cards.title: The serpent in the Garden of Eden

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Genesis 3:1–15 (Geneva 1599): the serpent deceives Eve, bringing sin and death into the world and earning God's curse.

cards.summary_basic: In Genesis, the serpent (understood by Shakespeare's readers as Satan in disguise) tempts Eve in the Garden of Eden, bringing sin, death, and exile from paradise. When the Ghost reveals that 'the serpent that did sting thy father's life / now wears his crown,' the murder in the orchard is cast in Eden's terms: Claudius is the satanic intruder, and the dead king an Adam dispossessed of his garden.
cards.detail_scholar: The Geneva Bible's marginal note glosses the serpent as the instrument of 'Satan.' Shakespeare reinforces the parallel by framing the murder in an 'orchard' (an enclosed garden) and by the Ghost's language of a paradise corrupted from within. The serpent-as-betrayer was among the most instantly legible biblical images for an Elizabethan audience.

cards.title: The Sixth Commandment and self-slaughter

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Exodus 20:13 (Geneva 1599): 'Thou shalt not kill.' Compare Deuteronomy 5:17.

cards.summary_basic: The commandment 'Thou shalt not kill' (the sixth in the Protestant numbering used in Shakespeare's England; the fifth in Catholic and Lutheran tradition) was understood in Elizabethan theology to forbid suicide as well as murder — killing oneself was 'self-slaughter,' a sin against God, who alone gives and takes life. The Church refused full Christian burial to suicides. This is why Hamlet says God 'fix'd / his canon 'gainst self-slaughter,' and why Ophelia's drowning is so anxiously debated in Act 5.
cards.detail_scholar: Here 'canon' means a divine law or decree (not a cannon). The doctrine that suicide damns the soul and forfeits consecrated burial gives weight to Hamlet's wish that his flesh would simply 'melt' — he is barred from hastening it. The theme returns at the graveside, where the priest grants Ophelia only 'maimed rites.'

cards.title: Cain and Abel: the first murder

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Genesis 4:1–16 (Geneva 1599): Cain kills his brother Abel; God sets a curse and a mark upon him.

cards.summary_basic: In Genesis, Cain murders his brother Abel out of envy — the first murder in the Bible, and a killing of brother by brother. Claudius (who murdered his brother, Hamlet's father) names his own crime through this story: 'It hath the primal eldest curse upon't, / A brother's murder.' In the graveyard the gravedigger jokes that a thrown skull is like 'Cain's jaw-bone, that did the first murder.'
cards.detail_scholar: The Bible does not say what weapon Cain used; the 'jawbone' is a medieval legend (probably borrowed from Samson's jawbone in Judges 15). The Cain story makes Claudius's fratricide resonate as the archetypal, God-cursed sin.

cards.title: Jephthah's daughter

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Judges 11:30–40 (Geneva 1599): Jephthah vows to sacrifice the first thing that greets him on return, and it is his only daughter.

cards.summary_basic: Jephthah, a judge of Israel, rashly vowed to God that if he won his battle he would sacrifice whatever first came out of his house to meet him — and it was his beloved only daughter. Hamlet taunts Polonius by calling him 'Jephthah, judge of Israel': a father whose folly will destroy his own daughter. It is a chilling forecast of what happens to Ophelia.

cards.title: The fall of a sparrow

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Matthew 10:29 (Geneva 1599): 'Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing, and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father?'

cards.summary_basic: Jesus tells his disciples that not even a sparrow — the cheapest of birds — falls to the ground without God's knowledge and will. Facing the duel he senses may kill him, Hamlet reaches a calm: 'we defy augury: there's a special providence in the fall of a sparrow.' He stops trying to read omens and accepts that the timing of death is in God's hands — 'the readiness is all.'
cards.detail_scholar: This is the play's clearest statement of Christian providence, and a turn away from the pagan revenge-tragedy machinery of omens and ghosts toward acceptance.

cards.title: Pilate washing his hands

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Matthew 27:24 (Geneva 1599): Pilate 'tooke water, and washed his handes before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just man.'

cards.summary_basic: When the crowd bayed for Jesus's death, the Roman governor Pontius Pilate publicly washed his hands to disown responsibility for the killing he was about to allow. At his deposition Richard flings the gesture back at the lords who claim clean hands in his fall: 'Though some of you, with Pilate, wash your hands, / Showing an outward pity; yet you Pilates / Have here deliver'd me to my sour cross' (4.1) — casting himself as a Christ betrayed and condemned.
cards.detail_scholar: Richard repeatedly likens his fall to Christ's Passion: he speaks of being sold by 'Judases' (the favourites, and Northumberland), of finding 'in twelve thousand none' faithful, and here of his 'sour cross.' The Pilate allusion turns the deposing lords into participants in a sacrilege — washing the hands cannot wash away the guilt of delivering up an anointed king. The futility of hand-washing as a cleansing of blood-guilt returns powerfully in Macbeth.

cards.title: The Prodigal Son

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Luke 15:11-32 (Geneva 1599); the husks the prodigal envies the swine at Luke 15:16.

cards.summary_basic: Jesus's parable of a younger son who demands his inheritance early, squanders it abroad in 'riotous living,' is reduced to feeding pigs and longing to eat their husks, then returns home in shame — where his father joyfully forgives him and kills the fatted calf to feast. The arc shadows Prince Hal, who seems to waste his youth among tavern thieves before returning to his royal father; Falstaff jokes that his ragged recruits look like 'prodigals lately come from swine-keeping, from eating draff and husks' (4.2).
cards.detail_scholar: Hal's soliloquy 'I know you all' (1.2) recasts his riot as a deliberate, temporary fall he will redeem — a planned prodigal's return staged for maximum effect. The parable was a stock subject of the painted cloths that hung in taverns and inns (Falstaff alludes to such hangings), making it doubly apt for the Eastcheap world. Shakespeare develops the prodigal motif further in Henry IV Part 2 and the rejection of Falstaff.

cards.title: Dives and Lazarus

source.name: Geneva Bible 1599
source.citation: Luke 16:19-31 (Geneva 1599); the rich man in purple and the beggar Lazarus whose sores the dogs licked.

cards.summary_basic: Jesus's parable of a rich man (traditionally called Dives, Latin for 'rich,' clothed in purple and feasting every day) and a starving beggar, Lazarus, covered in sores that dogs licked at the rich man's gate. Both die: Lazarus is carried to Abraham's bosom, the rich man to torment in hell-fire. Falstaff invokes both figures — his tattered conscripts are 'as ragged as Lazarus in the painted cloth, where the glutton's dogs licked his sores' (4.2), and he mocks Bardolph's fiery-red face as a reminder of 'Dives that lived in purple; for there he is in his robes, burning, burning' (3.3).
cards.detail_scholar: Like the Prodigal Son, the story was a common subject of cheap 'painted cloth' wall-hangings, which Falstaff repeatedly references; the joke assumes the audience can picture the standard image. Bardolph's flaming complexion as a memento mori of hell-fire is one of the play's running gags. 'Dives' is not a name in the Geneva text but the long-standing nickname for the rich man.
